en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Decisive Dhāraṇī, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly...]
The bhikṣus were all together, numbering twelve hundred and fifty, and there were eighty thousand bodhisattvas.

All were great sages who had attained mastery of supernatural powers; they were all non-retrogressive and had reached the ultimate realization of all dharmas. They had acquired dhāraṇīs and subtle eloquence, and were thoroughly proficient in the appropriate application of skillful means and expedients.

They have well studied the innumerable precepts of the bodhisattvas and entered into their profound essentials; they have realized and understood the convergence of the twelve links of dependent origination, practicing without fabrication, wherein emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are neither arising nor produced.

He causes all phenomena to enter the single path; he gathers and encompasses the treasury of the Dharma within the ocean of universal wisdom. His intention is vast and universal, his noble awakening is boundless, and he clearly understands the manifold meanings and discerns the intent of elegant phrases and verses.

When questioned, his answers were thorough and unimpeded; he understood the underlying intentions of sentient beings and liberated them from all fetters. His mind was equal to space, free from both hatred and love; having distanced himself from all defilements, he dwelt in tranquil and eternal peace, realizing the state of flawlessness and establishing the great field of the Mahāyāna.

He manifests the light of wisdom to subdue those of external teachings, just as the brilliance of the sun eclipses the glow of fireflies, mani-jewels, fire, and lightning; he utterly eliminates negligence and abandons all inverted views that calculate existence as either eternal or subject to annihilation.
Fully understanding that there is no self, no life-span, no vital principle, no person, and no nourisher, they observe with serene stillness all that arises.
For incalculable eons they have practiced the bodhisattva path, donned the armor of true virtue, transformed all beings through the six perfections, and cultivated the four debts of gratitude.

Through skillful means, they emerge from the path of birth and death; by this they guide the deluded masses, demonstrating calamity and fortune to rescue them from suffering and distress, so that they no longer create the roots of birth and death, and all may advance toward and enter the gate of samādhi.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Untroubled Head, Bodhisattva Lion’s Joy, Bodhisattva King of Radiant Glory, Bodhisattva Brahma-Sound Resounding Like Thunder and Rain, Bodhisattva Immeasurable Virtue Jewel, Bodhisattva Variegated Flowers, Bodhisattva Adorned with Various Necklaces, Bodhisattva King Grounded by Stone, Bodhisattva Dharma Rain, Bodhisattva King of the Lotus-Head Treasury, Bodhisattva Destroyer of Disgust for Emptiness, Bodhisattva Great Wisdom Radiance, and Bodhisattva King of Various Eloquences; there were eighty thousand such bodhisattvas as these.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of followers as he preached a sutra; the name of that dharma was "The Gate of the Resolving Dhāraṇī."

At that time, there were ten sons of noble family within the assembly who all listened together. Upon hearing the Tathāgata proclaim and resolve this gate of *dhāraṇī*, they were filled with joy and exultation, and wholesome states of mind arose within them. They cast off sleep and delighted in dwelling in seclusion; they cultivated the virtue of contentment and devoted themselves to walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Diligent day and night, they did not dare to be indolent, remaining free from negligence and thoughts of sensual desire. Thus, with such earnestness, they did not cease their diligent recitation for seven years. Yet, throughout those seven years, their minds wandered and they could not find even a moment’s rest; how much less could they attain the gate of *dhāraṇī*?

Failing to attain their aspirations, their minds became weary and disillusioned; they took pleasure in secluded dwelling and the practice of austerity, yet delighted in sleep and neglected diligent effort. They no longer practiced walking meditation or renounced sensual desires, nor did they again cultivate the gateway of *dhāraṇī*.

Having cast off the robes of a śramaṇa and abandoned the precepts to pursue a lowly life, their minds were deluded as they sought out the shortcomings of the holy teaching; they all returned to lay life and resumed the five worldly occupations.
At that time, the World-Honored One resolved King Ajātaśatru’s false doubts and removed his hesitations; for seven days he remained in silence, then manifested his sublime majesty.
Consequently, he caused the king to abandon negligence and the mind of contention, and to untie the knots of kingship and all bonds of frivolous views.
When the seven days had concluded, he went with seven hundred million people to the place where the Buddha was, desiring to receive the Dharma;
ten sons of noble family, including the youngest, also attended upon the king within the great assembly.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Fearless Practice (*Abhayacaryā*). He had attained *dhāraṇī*, and through countless kalpas he had perfected the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Having reached the state of non-arising and being free from inversion, his eloquence was immeasurable as he entered into all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). With the power of the path of right wisdom, he discerned and accorded with the practices of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and was enlightened regarding the inconceivable categories of *dhāraṇī* gates. He universally perceived the dispositions, natures, and faculties of all sentient beings and their lack of fixed destination; for those who were ready to be transformed, he preached the Dharma without losing its fundamental essence.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable One, God among Gods!

These ten sons of noble family have left the household life to practice the Way, exerting themselves day and night for seven years without slackening. Yet, though they sought the *dhāraṇī* of their aspirations, they did not obtain it; losing their original resolve, they cast off the robes of a śramaṇa and returned home to their worldly occupations, finding fault with the holy teaching.”

I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the meaning of the Dharma and, through skillful means, transform and enlighten them as is appropriate, so that these sons of noble family may reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future, and shall take refuge in the Unsurpassed Great Way.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:

"This son of good family, in the distant past, during ages long gone by, slandered and reviled the Buddha-dharma and refused to listen to or accept it. Because he slandered and transgressed against the Buddha-dharma, as a result of this, he was unable to swiftly attain the unsurpassed Great Way."
The Bodhisattva Fearless Practice then addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"I have heard that the Honored One among Men, The Dharma King, has proclaimed the Radiance;
The practices of all Bodhisattvas Are able to eliminate the sins of *aṅga*."
His meritorious virtues and wisdom are spread far and wide, such that none can surpass him.
His ten powers are peerless, and his noble wisdom is unimpeded;
having already been liberated from the three realms, he never again succumbs to negligence.
Pray, speak of their conduct so that they may purify this path of practice.
Now that I have been inspired by the Infinite One, I hold fast to the wisdom of the nectar of immortality;
I shall now explain it in detail for those whose minds are entangled in the web of doubt.
I now inquire of the Tathāgata; O World-Honored One, pray resolve this for me:
What is it that causes the various bodhisattvas, practicing the Mahāyāna, to be constantly diligent day after day and to never slacken in their most supreme conduct?
Having subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, having incinerated all defilements and impurities,
and having understood all modes of conduct, you manifest this to sentient beings.
Pray, explain for us in detail the fundamental practice of the Way.
His words are most subtle and refined; with a serene countenance, he speaks for the sake of others.
Abiding within the realm of birth and death, he delights in delivering beings from the afflictions of beginning and end.
Listen attentively to these praised instructions, which resolve all doubts.
I most earnestly pray that you will expound for us the practice of the path as it should be cultivated;
through the pure cultivation of virtuous qualities, may our fundamental conduct extinguish birth and death.
Out of compassion, grant us peace and security, so as to deliver the minds of all sentient beings.
Relinquishing and abandoning all possessions, Bestowing precious treasures and vehicles,
Giving away one's head and eyes to others, And likewise with wife and children;
Reverently practicing patience, Delighting in the virtue of the precepts.
Diligently cultivating the vow for tranquility, he clearly understands his firm resolve;
by virtue of these qualities, the assembly is able to endure hundreds of thousands of afflictions.
Wherever the Benevolent Honored One treads, his supreme skillful means are unimpeded.
Clearly knowing what ought to be practiced, acting with seasonal precision and without hesitation, one extinguishes the three defilements; thus, there is no limit to what can be achieved.
Discerning the work of renunciation, one brings transformation and enlightenment to those in the five realms of existence.
"Abide securely and speak only for their sake; you should practice the path as is appropriate.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:
"These ten sons of noble family were, in a past life, offenders against the Buddhas and slanderers of the scriptures."
What is meant by violating the Dharma of all Buddhas?

In the distant past, long ago, after passing through thirty-two kalpas in the world-system called Jvalanaprabha, there was a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
These ten sons of noble family were born as the sons of great and wealthy elders in that world. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they remained among those at the beginning of their studies;

for the sake of their World-Honored One, they established meritorious works, constructing five hundred stūpas, temples, lecture halls, and vihāras. With various kinds of offerings, they provided all the bhikṣu-saṃghas with everything they required; in every vihāra within each of those stūpas and temples, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus dwelt and practiced.

“At that time in that world, there was a bodhisattva named Vidyutkūṭa (辯積), who had attained dhāraṇī and mastery of skillful means; he transformed all beings according to their needs through his advances and retreats, and ascended a high seat to preach the Dharma appropriately for each.”

Five hundred Buddhas bestowed upon him the eloquence of instruction, while eighty billion devaputras remained in the void, purifying all impurities and providing magnificent adornments. They conjured a lecture hall, erected various banners and streamers, and made offerings to the Dharma Master. Out of compassion for all beings, he preached the sutra; seventy thousand people attained the stage of non-retrogression and shall achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, while another ten thousand attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
"At that time, there was a king in that world named Candradatta (Moon-Giver), who delighted in the Dharma and thirsted for the meaning of the sutras, finding joy in the Dharma itself.

At that time, the king made offerings to the Dharma Master Bodhisattva Vādibhūti (Accumulation of Eloquence) together with his inner court, noble ladies, and a retinue of five hundred women. He performed great musical performances and scattered flowers made of jewels over him; he anointed his body with sandalwood incense, covered him with five hundred parasols, and offered five hundred exquisite garments. For seven days and nights, he remained standing and did not dare to sit. He provided for his comfort according to what was appropriate, never missing the proper timing. His reverence for the Dharma Master was unsurpassed; his exalted honor and merit were beyond compare."

At that time, the son of a wealthy and noble elder slandered and falsely accused the Dharma Master Bodhisattva Bianji, claiming that he had violated the Dharma and the precepts and did not follow the practice of the prohibitions.
Because of these offenses, they shall fall into hell for a full ninety thousand years;
when born among humans, for fifty thousand lifetimes they shall fall among the borderlands and barbarians, their minds deluded by false views and shrouded by the veil of sin;
for six hundred lifetimes they shall always be born blind, mute and tongueless, unable to speak.

Having left the household life to become a śramaṇa for the sake of the Way, he practiced with diligent effort for seven hundred lifetimes; yet, not sparing even his own body or life, he failed to attain dhāraṇī.
Now, having been born again in my world, his mind is repeatedly distracted and unable to achieve single-minded concentration.
For this reason, because they are obscured by the veil of karmic retribution from their past lives, these sons of noble family have not yet attained the dhāraṇīs.

Therefore, O worthy one, I entrust you with this matter and solemnly charge you: upon hearing this sutra and meeting a Dharma teacher in person, you should proclaim it for others and offer them all joint worship; you must not harbor grief or harbor malice in your hearts, much less give rise to evil thoughts upon hearing of it from afar!
The Buddha said, “Noble son!
Suppose there were someone who took all sentient beings and gouged out both their eyes; although this sin is heavy, it can still be exhausted once the kalpas have run their course.”
If one harbors harmful intentions toward a Dharma teacher, the kalpas of retribution for that sin will exceed even those [previously mentioned].
Suppose there were someone who took all sentient beings prone to strife and quarreling, reconciled their separations, and brought them widespread peace and security;

yet, if one sees a Dharma teacher and dwells before him with a single-minded heart, these merits exceed those of reconciling sentient beings in conflict and bringing them peace by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and a trillionfold—they cannot compare to the joy of dwelling before a Bodhisattva with a pleasant countenance.
Why is this? Those who slander the Dharma Master slander the Tathāgata.

Those who wish to make offerings to the Tathāgata should honor the Dharma Master; those who wish to revere the Tathāgata should follow the Dharma Master; and those who wish to pay homage to the Tathāgata should pay homage to the Dharma Master.

Why is this so? All bodhisattvas are born from the Dharma; through the bodhisattvas, all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is accomplished; and by means of all-knowledge, one becomes a Buddha, a World-Honored One.

The Bodhisattva’s arising of the aspiration for enlightenment is such that he does not pay homage by dwelling in desire or remaining amidst the afflictions; because there is nothing produced, there is no place of abiding, and thus his pure cultivation of the Brahma-faring merits the salutation of homage. He does not pay homage to the formless realm through the meditative attainment of the formless samādhi.
One does not take birth through the influence of residual karmic retribution; rather, one attains mastery over one's vows and is born according to those very vows.

Having already attained liberation from all the deluded and ignorant conduct of ordinary beings, to claim that a Bodhisattva could possess residual karmic retribution would be like claiming that empty space possesses form and appearance.
For example, son of good family!

When the Naga King Anavatapta wishes to see the various nagas sporting, he instructs and informs all his naga retinues: "All of you rely upon the Naga King to obtain peace and security; you shall always be freed from the three kinds of suffering and remain free from affliction."

In this way, the bodhisattva relinquishes all pleasure, severs the offenses of the three bases, extinguishes the hindrances and defilements, and destroys all suffering and affliction; only then does he bring peace and deliverance to sentient beings.
Just as a dragon roams within the water without any fear, so too does the Bodhisattva roam through the triple world without any dread.
Just as a dragon moves through deep waters, seeing all that exists therein and indulging its desires at will, yet remains unharmed and undisturbed by the water; so it is with the Bodhisattva.

In this way, the bodhisattva wanders among the masses of blind and ignorant ordinary people; abiding in their conduct, he observes only the deliberations of wisdom and does not deviate from the practice of the Way. He does not associate with fools to share in their defilements, nor is he submerged by what is seen in the three realms.
Therefore, a practitioner should always protect and uphold the Dharma with composure; this is the practice cultivated by a Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Those who wish to take refuge in the Buddha, And reverently receive the teachings of the immeasurable Sages,
I have always made offerings to the Bodhisattvas and revered the Teacher.
The robes and bowl I now wear, as well as my bed, couch, and various sitting mats—
Buddha has accepted these as offerings and permitted me to give them to those who are resolved in the Way.
The lamps offered to the Buddhas— by providing such lamps to them—
one thus attains perfect enlightenment, becoming the most supreme among all sages.
By giving food, drink, and vehicles, these wise ones [attain the same].
As a guide for the ignorant, he leads them toward the realm of ambrosia.
To all classes of sentient beings, he bestows peace among devas and humans;
yet, even by following his initial resolve, one cannot repay his kindness.
The Bodhisattva Fearless Practice again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens!
Is there perhaps some skillful means by which these ten sons of noble family may eliminate their transgressions and reach the Way?"
The Buddha said:

"Suppose these ten people were to single-mindedly receive and study what the Buddha has proclaimed; if they cultivate this Dharma and Vinaya and become śramaṇas, and diligently recite these dhāraṇī verses, they shall attain the Way."
What are the dhāraṇī verses? They are:
"Cultivate purity and clarity; The phrase of fresh and stainless purity; Pure and cool, Without bestowing, and without creating;
Without anything to be attained; Following with swiftness, One takes up new birth."
Revering diligence, honoring conduct and gait, Exerting oneself in practice, with wisdom clearly understanding,
Mastering observation, arising from nothingness, Departing from affliction and hardship, one wanders in ease and comfort.
"Exalted, light, and easy, universally pure, there is nothing impure.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:

"These ten persons, by reciting these dhāraṇī verses, shall for seven days cultivate meritorious virtue without becoming dejected or losing their composure; they shall harbor no anger, remain tranquil and soon roam in non-action, possess a heart free from blemish, maintain equanimity toward all things, and, detached from the five aggregates, abandon impure thoughts while recollecting the Buddha."
"O sons of noble family!

If you can thus reverently follow and uphold the Way of the Buddha, there shall be a thousand Buddhas in each of the worlds of the ten directions who will manifest before you so that you may see them for yourselves. By disciplining your mind and reproaching yourself, and by taking refuge in the Holy Honored Ones, your transgressions and calamities may be eliminated, and you shall attain the wisdom of the Way."
"Sons of good family!

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching and in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya, they immediately abandoned their household affairs and went forth as śramaṇas. They recited these dhāraṇī verses, practicing them with diligence day and night for seven days just as the Sage had instructed. When the seven days were completed, they immediately saw a thousand Buddhas in each of the ten directions, who explained to them individually the karmic practices for the elimination of offenses."

At that time, they all attained the gate of the dhāraṇī for practicing universal wisdom, transcended the hardships of birth and death for thirty-six kalpas, reached the stage of non-retrogression, and shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:
"The King Candradatta of that time is none other than the present Amitābha;
as for that Vāgasaṃcaya, he is the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."
The ten sons of the elder are none other than these ten men of noble lineage here today.
Therefore, do not act with timidity!

Those who are resolved to study the Bodhisattva Vehicle should diligently practice according to the Buddha’s instructions, abide in the True Dharma, abandon ignorance, and carefully refrain from seeking out the faults of others.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:
"There are four practices which, if one can follow and cultivate them, will purify and adorn the path to Buddhahood.
What are these four?"
First, to practice the matter of emptiness, always maintaining a heart of compassion and not harming sentient beings;
second, for a bodhisattva to pity and respect their fellow students and not treat them with contempt;
third, to preach the Dharma for others as a gift of lightness, without harboring any expectations.
The fourth is: the will is always single-minded, without harboring thoughts of receiving offerings of food or clothing.
These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"His resolve is always joyful and firmly believes in emptiness and non-existence;
he cultivates the pure and most supreme path, which shines forth according to the season like the light of the sun, yet once the Buddha-way is attained, its illumination surpasses that."
No one has ever known his flaws; as a person of holy virtue, he universally endures all things.
In such a field of purity and gentleness, he has cast aside arrogance and is capable of bearing the immeasurable.
All manner of supreme and exquisite garments should always be given as alms to those who are resolved upon the Buddha-way;
furthermore, one should not hope for offerings from others—this is the pure category of the Buddha-way.
By bestowing immeasurable Dharma without seeking or hoping for reward, constantly cultivating compassion and mindfulness toward all sentient beings,
and always maintaining a disposition that cherishes the principle of gratitude— this is what constitutes the adornment and purification of the path of all Buddhas.

If one would joyfully revere all the sages, and if one desires to make offerings to the scriptures of desirelessness, one should always serve the infinite Buddha-way; for these Three Jewels are all born from within it.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:
"Furthermore, there are four things by which one swiftly attains the Way of the Buddha.
What are these four? They are as follows:"
First, to love and delight in the clear scriptures and take pleasure in the Mahāyāna;
second, to remain far removed from sensual desires and not practice negligence;
third, to constantly cultivate the means of rescuing the poor and destitute by providing them with what they lack.
The fourth is to be able to generate the seven types of Dharma-wealth and bestow them upon others. These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Delighting in the Dharma Master, aspiring to the Mahāyāna, far removed from sensual desires and practicing pure conduct,
compassionating those in distress and poverty, rescuing all from peril and difficulty,
and constantly bestowing the seven riches upon those who do not slacken in the Path."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:
"Furthermore, there are four things by which one quickly attains the Way of the Buddha.
What are these four? They are as follows:"
First, to constantly practice great kindness (*maitrī*), feeling compassion for all living beings;
second, to constantly practice great compassion (*karuṇā*), shedding tears on their behalf;
third, to constantly practice great joy (*muditā*), looking upon sentient beings with a harmonious and pleasant countenance.
The fourth is to constantly practice great protection, rescuing and delivering beings from the afflictions of birth and death within the three realms.
These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Constantly practicing great loving-kindness, he takes pity on all classes of sentient beings;
mindful of bringing them to fulfillment, he is like a mother nurturing her child.
With great compassion, he traverses from beginning to end, undaunted by any calamities or hardships.”
The five realms of existence are like foam and bubbles; out of compassion for them, he sheds tears.
With a serene countenance, he observes all sentient beings and delights them with the Dharma, showing them how to leave behind all suffering and attain a state of painless, eternal peace.

"Appearing in a languid manner, he follows the five destinies; through skillful means, he demonstrates what is appropriate for each, enabling beings to cross beyond the afflictions of the three realms and attain the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice:

“If there are those who diligently seek this dhāraṇī, they should practice dwelling in seclusion and frequently attend Dharma assemblies; they should maintain pure conduct, wear clean clothing, and further observe the four bases of deportment and the correctness of ritual etiquette without slackening their resolve. With various kinds of offerings, they should support the Dharma Master and have deep faith in the Triple Gem.”

They always maintain reverence, humility, and docility; they never grow weary or indolent but constantly practice diligence; they are free from the karma of flattery and deviant conduct; and their thoughts are never apart from the Buddha.

That which the mind reveres and cultivates is the understanding of non-existence; having realized non-existence, one is free from conceptualization. One is able to fully comprehend the nature and conduct of sentient beings, diligently exercising self-restraint so that mind and speech are in accord. One delights in the Buddhas, inquiring and receiving their teachings, admonishing transgressions, maintaining integrity, and encouraging the roots of virtue. One’s dignified demeanor and ritual propriety do not deviate from the Way and its teachings.

There is neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate; upon hearing the voices of non-humans, one does not become terrified, nor does one fear snakes, vipers, or venomous stinging insects. One reveres and honors teachers and elders, cultivating this sutra without ever becoming weary or indolent.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, thirty thousand people who had not previously awakened the mind for the Way now all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment;
five thousand people became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;
and thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas.
The Buddha said:
“If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra-dharma, attain the full perfection of all meritorious virtues and immeasurable eloquence;

or if sons of good family and daughters of good family who study the bodhisattva path were to fill the three-thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and offer them to the Triple Gem for as many eons as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges.”
If someone hears this sutra, their merit and honor will surpass that [of the former].

Even if a bodhisattva were to practice the five perfections for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet lacked great wisdom and skillful means, it would not equal hearing the essentials of this sutra; their merit and honor would surpass that [of the former].
Therefore, son of good family!

I entrust this sutra to you and commit it to your care. You must earnestly encourage and assist one another, protecting it at all times so that it is not forgotten or lost. Ensure that it remains in the world without being increased or diminished, upholding, reciting, and reading it, and extensively explaining its meaning for others.
"Even if you should encounter misfortune and lose your life, you must carefully preserve this sutra and never allow it to be forgotten or lost;
this is the teaching of the Buddha.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Fearless Practice (Abhaya-caryā), the ten sons of noble family, all the great śrāvakas, and the entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and worldly humans—heard the sutra with joy, prostrated themselves, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Definitive Dhāraṇī Spoken by the Buddha
